notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1382.tmp1382.opp-lat: Line 2: 'sancti Maurilii super Sarrae Ramen' read as 'sancti Mauritii super Sarrae flumen' (St Maurice on the river Saar). 'quod et fecit Cunibertus' is awkward in the Latin; rendered as Cunibert also subscribing. Line 5: 'parere impero' read as 'parere imperio' (cf. the parallel in diploma III), giving 'obey our command [and our lord Arnulf's]'; translated loosely to fit the clause. Words in square brackets in diploma II are the edition's brackets (passages absent from some copies or suspected), not translator's additions. Line 8: 'numine' read as 'nomine'. The datings by the Incarnation and the titles 'archbishop' and 'duke of Mosellan Austrasia' are anachronistic for the 620s; these diplomas are generally regarded as later fabrications, but are translated as given.

Words in round brackets in IV are the edition's variant readings from another witness, and bracketed remarks in V and VI are the edition's own notes; both are kept as printed. Footnote letters are omitted. Scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'tegis' for 'regis', 'Jecrevimus' for 'decrevimus'). In IV, 'Huniberti' is presumably Cunibert of Cologne. 'excepto stipe et comitatu' is uncertain: 'stipe' may mean a levy or tribute. 'intraha/Jutraha' is unidentified. In V the Merovingian Latin is very irregular and the bronze-tablet text has gaps; the opening sentence is anacoluthic in the original. 'Ferrarias', 'Leubaredo', 'Eudoncovilla' and 'Roteneco' are left unidentified. 'optol.' is taken as 'obtulit' (presented). In VI, 'aeditibus/aedilibus' is read as 'aedibus' (household).

VII: 'garantia' is taken as madder (warantia); 'Vicarii' in the list of payers is taken as Vicani, 'men of Wic' (Wicus portus, probably Quentovic); 'ex pane nostra' read as 'ex parte nostra'; 'nestram' as 'nostram'. Several toll names (vultatici, passionatici, themonatici, chespetatici, mestatici, laudatici, salutatici) are of uncertain sense and are left untranslated. VIII: the phrase 'a praepositis nostro militum profectori' is garbled; 'officer ... leader of soldiers' is a guess. The dating formulas and content are anachronistic for 630, and the charter is generally regarded as spurious. Praevalia, Pravanum, Mons Julius and Oscela are left in their Latin forms. X: the witness list is corrupt: 'Mercensis' read as Metensis (Metz), 'Nomomensis' as Noviomensis (Noyon), 'Aurifalo' as aurifabri (goldsmith, i.e. Eligius); 'Louis son of Dagobert' is anachronistic. XI: 'Tricena pons' and 'Luvera' are not securely identified (the latter is perhaps the Louvre); 'AEgynayvi' is an unidentified, probably corrupt, name.

Editor's variant readings (Chop., Samm./Sammarth., Labb.) are kept in brackets as in the edition; stray footnote letters omitted. XII: 'laidis' read as leudes (royal followers); 'votatur' read as vocatur; 'pago Maiginensi' (Maifeld?) not certainly identified. XIII: 'parte menti' read as 'parte menti' = part of the chin (perhaps for mentum); uncertain. 'ditioni ... dominicae' rendered as demesne lordship. The parenthesis marks follow the edition and do not close cleanly; the syntax of the anathema is anacoluthic in the Latin. The dating elements (indiction 6 for 632) are inconsistent, and this charter is generally regarded as spurious.

Stray letters after words (a, b, c, h, i, etc.) are footnote marks and are omitted. In XV, 'Volum' read as 'Votum' (vow). The date 'sexingentesimo tredecimo' (613) conflicts with the heading's 633 and with Dagobert's reign; translated as printed. The opening parenthesis in XV ('qui qualiter...') closes only at 'redii' as in the edition. Place names in both diplomas (Kannis, Cressiacum, Decima, Rubera, Leder, Kirckhaim, Marley, Corona Virdenheim, Vege, Mosellus) are kept in their printed forms; Decima is probably Detzem and Rubera the Ruwer, but these are not certain. 'Hubis' rendered 'hides' (Hufen, units of land). The Haslach diploma and its vision narrative are generally regarded as later forgeries.

XVI: the bracketed 'M. B.' variants are reproduced as the edition gives them. 'Nemetensis' is taken as Speyer (Nemetes). 'monelam' read as 'monetam'; 'tribula' as 'tributa'; 'babere' as 'habere'; 'heneficium' as 'beneficium'; 'placitam' as 'placitum'. 'ministeriales' left untranslated as a technical term. XVII: the text breaks after 'more....' (a verb such as 'venabamur' seems lost; the edition marks 'Sic in apog.'). 'nive inculpatam terrae' is obscure; rendered as the cross image in snow on unmarked ground, tentatively. 'Gallis-Villa', 'Bellumvillare' and 'ripparii curtis' left unidentified. 'Gavalitane' taken as the see of the Gabali (Javols/Mende). The phrase 'ipso obnoxius orante' is rendered loosely as 'at his own humble request'. The diploma is generally regarded as spurious.

Stray footnote letters (e.g. 'Dionysiic', 'Argenteriasb', 'monasteriumd', 'matricularios c', 'nostri a', 'quadragesimo a') omitted. Clipiacum taken as Clichy, as with Clepiacum in the glossary. XIX: the dating 'indictione XII, XIII' is evidently elliptical; taken as the 13th regnal year. The river Magneuria is unidentified. XX: 'ex prae lone' read as 'ex praedone' (a robber); 'Maurosus' appears to be a byname. The place names Bavia, Railhiez, Elpra, Aetimundi, Baileporis, Brolium, Mansilium, Clarus Voionus, Wiellemanus, Wilheis, Gomundus, Merdosus Voionus and Ducio are left in their Latin forms. This charter is generally regarded as spurious: compare the dating by the Incarnation and the anachronistic chancery. XXI: the main verb of the long sentence 'pro mercedis nostrae compendium ipsas Sarclidas...' is missing, and '[given]' has been supplied. 'noncupante' read as 'nuncupatam', 'freciis' as 'fredis', and 'iu' as 'in'. The bracketed '[Editi habent Sarclitas]' is the editor's note and is translated as it stands.

Footnote letters after words (e.g. Dionysiid, Dodone e, Clipiaco a) omitted. XXII: 'Homo semper et incolumis etiam, et ac si' is awkward and may be corrupt; translated for the evident sense. 'ut soliditate' read as 'et soliditate'. XXIII: 'eligimus' perhaps for 'elegimus'; the edition marks two gaps ('Sic in Editis'), so the sentence about penalties is incomplete; 'deputare' is supplied by the edition. XXIV: the dating 'eighth year of our reign' does not agree with the heading's year 635 (fourteenth year); the bracketed variant notes from the royal cartulary are the editor's and are kept as in the text. Place names Aquaputa, Tauriacum, Tibernio, Rubridum, Monarvilla, Vasconis Vallis and Molliacum left in their Latin forms (not securely identified here); Molliacum appears as Malliacus in the next charter.

Line 52: the heading names the estate Molliacum, the text Malliacus. Line 53: the basilica of Vincent at Paris is the later Saint-Germain-des-Prés; Cumbis villa, Dravernum, Braunate and Grande Campum are left in their Latin forms as uncertain identifications. Line 55: 'timore nudus' read as 'stripped of fear'; 'nune' read as 'nunc', 'politur' as 'potitur', 'Illi' as 'illis', 'hac duae' as 'hae duae'. Patriagus/Patriacus, the rivers Jugia, Vulsia, Conus and the 'fons Maer', and most estate names could not be securely identified and are kept in Latin. 'extra capellam nostram' rendered 'besides our chapel'; it may mean 'outside'. Dado (Ouen) appears here as archbishop of Rouen, an anachronism for 636 suggesting the charter is not authentic.

XXVIII: 'Chipiaco' read as Clipiaco (Clichy). XXIX: the text is badly damaged, with many lacunae and blank spaces; it is in heavily vulgar Latin, and the translation of the fragments is tentative; 'dom.' is taken as domesticus, and 'Dado optol.' is read as Dado obtulit; the final words are read as Clipiaco feliciter. XXX: 'vince' is read as vineae. XXXI: the editor's notes give variants from another copy: 'visi sumus' (for the confirmation clause), 'nos et nostri' in place of 'vos juniores', the negation 'non' omitted, 'sed' for 'nisi', and 'eleemosiniis pauperum'. Mummolus is called prefect here but the dating 'anno secundo' sits oddly with the other diplomas.

XXXII: the edition's bracketed variants (mostly from Doublet) are omitted; notable ones are 'effectum' for 'affectum', 'quilibet episcopus vel archiepiscopus', and the dating 'second year' at Compiègne rather than 'tenth year' at Paris. Parentheses mark the additions to the earlier diploma. XXXIII: 'exerceat' read as 'exercens' per the edition; 'nara' read as 'nam', 'fram' as 'iram', 'illus' as 'illius', 'eum gemitibus' as 'cum gemitibus'. For 'affuisse' Doublet has 'non abfuisse' (same sense). Place-names are left as given except Ruilliacum (Reuilly), Telum (Theols, probable) and Arnon. The twenty-fifth regnal year is incompatible with 637; the charter is widely regarded as spurious.

XXXIV: the Latin is badly constructed; 'matricularios presentialiter perveniant' and the clause on the xenodochium and 'Saclitas/Sarditas' are obscure and rendered tentatively. Date 'VII decimo Kal. Octobris' taken as the seventeenth day before the Kalends; the regnal year XVI conflicts with the year 637 given in the heading. XXXV: the sentence 'ideo quod ibidem devotissimus ... visi fuimus concessisse' and the final purpose clause ('pro intercessione ... mercedem, quod agerentur') are corrupt; 'ra' is probably a scanning error. 'Sauriciagore' is an unidentified place name, probably corrupt. XXXVI: 'Spinogilo' taken as Épinay(-sur-Seine); regnal year XXX is impossible for Dagobert. XXXVII: 'testamentum mancipiorum' perhaps for 'statum'; 'et eorumdem mancipiorum ... teneatur' is elliptical. Stray letters (a, b, c, f) are footnote marks and are omitted.

XXXIX: 'Vigenna' and 'Vienna' are taken as the Vienne; Plumbata, Aula, Ternant, Cursous, Odriacum, Maleredum, Antigniacum, Selignech, Pleis and Buymet are left unidentified; 'a duello' (fleeing from a duel?) is obscure. Ingrandes and Dangé are probable identifications. The garbled 'quarum vicum' follows the bracketed correction. XL: 'slavis' is probably an error for 'servis'. The diploma is generally regarded as spurious: Arnulf as 'of Metz' alongside Pippin 'of Neustria', and the date 640 against the heading's 637, are inconsistent. 'cambutta' is taken as a pastoral staff and 'subtalares' as shoes.

nodes.text: THE ECCLESIASTICAL DIPLOMAS OF DAGOBERT I, KING OF THE FRANKS
(Bréquigny, Diplomata, vol. II, new edition, from which the notes are also taken.)
I. Diploma of Dagobert I, by which he hands over the abbey of St Maurice, or the monastery of Tholey, to the church of St Peter at Trier (year 622).

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen. Dagobert, by the ordaining clemency of God, king of the Franks. It is done with prudent consideration that the record of dispositions or exchanges is committed to the memory of sacred letters, since by the presence of writing the mist of forgetfulness is removed, and the wickedness of those who plot evil is destroyed. Therefore let the diligence of all the faithful of God's holy Church, both present and future, know that the apostolic man our Father, lord Modoald, archbishop of Trier, approached the height of our serenity, begging that we should hand over a certain abbey of St Maurice the martyr, which is called the monastery of Tholey, built by us and situated by the river Saar in the duchy called Mosellan Austrasia, to the church of St Peter, prince of the apostles, which is known to be built in the city of Trier, where the principal seat of his bishopric is recognised to be, to the honour of God and of his saints who rest there; and at once, wishing gladly to satisfy his fitting request out of reverence for him, we decreed that it should be so done. We have also given the same abbey in its entire integrity to the church of the aforesaid see, for the perpetual commemoration of King Chilperic of blessed memory, our grandfather, and of Chlothar our father, and of our paternal kin, namely Chilperic and Chlothar, most Christian kings, and of our own soul, with churches, vineyards, fields, men, roads, things acquired and to be acquired, movables and immovables, and with all their appurtenances and adjacent lands. And for the aforesaid churches, and for the Father of the brothers of the aforesaid cell of St Maurice built on the river Saar, we have appointed as protector, ruler and advocate the illustrious lord, lord Chlodulf, duke of Mosellan Austrasia, son of Duke Arnulf, born of royal blood. All these things, therefore, by this present precept of our authority, we give and hand over to belong forever to the often-mentioned see, on this condition: that the aforesaid bishop and his successors should have for all time the same power over the aforementioned abbey as over the other affairs of the same bishopric, to dispose of everything securely as they please, according to the advantage of that church, so that it may please the rulers of the same see, with all the clergy subject to their rule, always to implore the mercy of God both for us and for our aforesaid predecessors and for the appointed protector. May this authority of our donation, with no successor of ours ever breaking in upon it, obtain in the name of God the most solid stability through all the ages of the turning world; and, strengthened by our safeguard, we have confirmed it below with our hand, together with Duke Chlodulf, as Cunibert, archbishop of Cologne, also did, and we have ordered it to be sealed with the impressions of our rings. Given on the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord's Incarnation 622. Done at Metz, in the royal palace, in the name of God, happily.
Dagobert, king of the Franks. Cunibert, archbishop of Cologne. Chlodulf, duke of Mosellan Austrasia.
II.

Diploma of Dagobert I, by which he confirms the property of the church of St Peter at Trier; orders the cell of St Hilary, or of St Maximin, to remain under the right of this church; and gives to both as advocate Arnulf, duke of Mosellan Austrasia (year 623).

[In the name of the Lord, amen.] Dagobert, king of the Franks, to the illustrious [Arnulf, duke of Mosellan Austrasia, and the other] dukes, counts, domestici, and all agents both beyond and on this side of the Rhine, the Loire and the Moselle, absent as well as present. We believe that it undoubtedly makes, in the name of our God, for the increase and stability of our kingdom, if we bring to effect the petitions of priests and the right requests of churches which they have laid open to our ears. Therefore the apostolic man our Father Modoald, archbishop of Trier, presented before our eyes a precept of our predecessors, the earlier kings, our kinsmen, Sigebert, Theudebert, Theuderic, and indeed of Chlothar of good memory and remembrance, the glorious king, our father, strengthened by their hands, in which it was set down that not only our same father but also the aforesaid kings his predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks, confirmed by the authority of their seals whatever properties good and holy men had assigned, with a view to divine contemplation, to the share of the church of St Peter at Trier, so that their kingdom might be protected by heavenly aid, and afterwards they might rejoice with Christ in the heavenly kingdom with a blessed end. For the firmness of the matter the same aforesaid bishop Modoald besought our highness that, following the custom of our father and predecessors, we should order a precept of authority of this kind to be made concerning the same properties, for the love of God and reverence for St Peter. To his petition we gladly gave assent, and we decreed that this precept of our authority be made for that church, for love of divine worship and the remedy of our soul. By it we command and order that all properties or resources belonging to the church of St Peter of the city of Trier, namely the cell of St Hilary, which is now called the cell of St Maximin, which is built on the estate of St Peter, castles, villages, estates, vineyards, woods, men, or whatever, by the bounty of divine clemency, may hereafter accrue to increase that church, situated about the Rhine, the Loire [or the Moselle] river in our kingdom, shall all remain perpetually bound under the right and power of the church of St Peter at Trier and of its bishop. [For the better observance of this matter, and so that the properties of the aforesaid churches, namely of blessed Peter and of blessed Maximin, may be kept in prosperity, lest any trouble be inflicted on them hereafter by marauders, we give to the aforesaid church of blessed Peter of the city of Trier, and to the brothers of the aforesaid cell of blessed Hilary, which is now called the cell of St Maximin, which is built on the estate of St Peter, as protector, ruler and advocate the illustrious lord, lord Arnulf, born of royal blood, our kinsman and tutor, duke of Mosellan Austrasia, whom we command to observe all these things faithfully.] Therefore in like manner we decree that none of the [dukes], public judges, or anyone of judicial power, should place obstacles in the monastery, about the churches, cells, villages, fields, men, or other places, but that it be permitted to the said bishop and his successors to possess all the aforesaid things in full for all time in quiet order, for the remedy of our soul and of our kinsmen, as is contained in the precept of our most pious father; and I command that they faithfully obey ours [and our lord Arnulf's]. But so that this precept of our authority may obtain fuller force in the name of God, and may be more truly believed by the faithful of God's holy mother Church, namely in present and future times, and be more diligently preserved by our successors, we have confirmed it below with our own hand, [with our princes,] and have ordered it to be sealed [with the impressions of our rings]. [Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, in the year from the Lord's incarnation 623.]
Dagobert, king of the Franks. Cunibert, archbishop of Cologne. Atto, bishop of Metz. Principius, bishop of Speyer. [Arnulf, duke of Mosellan Austrasia.] Pippin, mayor of the palace [duke of Hesbaye].
III.

Diploma of Dagobert I, by which he confirms the property of the church of St Peter at Trier; orders the cell of blessed Eucharius, or of St Matthias, to remain under the right of this church; and gives to both as advocate Arnulf, duke of Mosellan Austrasia (year 623).

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Dagobert, by the favour and ordering of divine providence, king of the Franks. It befits any person in authority, and most of all royal chief men, to comply with the prayers of the humble and moderate who live under religion, and to foster their quiet and peace as far as possible, and afterwards to safeguard it. Therefore let the discernment of all our faithful, both present and future, know that the venerable and apostolic man our Father, lord Modoald, archbishop of the holy Church of Trier, presented before our eyes a precept of the earlier kings of the Franks, in which it was set down that [our] predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks, confirmed by the authority of their decrees all properties whatever that good and holy men had assigned, with a view to divine contemplation, to the share of the church of St Peter at Trier, and gave upright dukes as protectors and advocates, so that their kingdom might be protected by heavenly aid, and afterwards they might reign in heaven with Christ the king of kings. For the truth and firmness of the matter the aforesaid bishop Modoald requested our highness that, following the customs of our father and predecessor kings, we should order a precept of authority of this kind to be made concerning the same properties, for the love of God and reverence for St Peter, and should give them a protector or advocate. To this petition we gladly gave consent, and we decreed that this precept of our authority and protection be made for that church, for love of divine worship and the remedy of our soul. By it we command and order that all resources or properties belonging to the church of St Peter of the city of Trier, namely the cell of St Eucharius, which is now called the cell of St Matthias the apostle, which is built in the territory of St Peter, prince of the apostles, castles, villages, estates, vineyards, woods, men, or whatever, by the bounty of divine clemency, may hereafter accrue to increase the same church, situated about the rivers Rhine, Loire or Moselle in our kingdom, shall all remain perpetually bound under the right and power of the church of St Peter at Trier and of its bishop. For the better observance of this matter, and so that the properties of the aforesaid churches may be kept in prosperity, namely lest any trouble be inflicted hereafter by marauders on the churches of blessed Peter and blessed Eucharius, we give to the aforesaid church of blessed Peter of the city of Trier, and to the brothers of the aforesaid cell of blessed Eucharius, which is now called the cell of St Matthias the apostle, which is built on the estate of St Peter, as protector, ruler and advocate the illustrious lord, lord Arnulf, born of royal blood, and our tutor, duke of Mosellan Austrasia, whom we command to observe all these things faithfully. Moreover in like manner we decree that none of the dukes, public judges, or anyone of judicial power, should place obstacles in the monastery, about the churches, cells, villages, fields, men, or other places, but that it be permitted to the said bishop and his successors to possess all the aforesaid things in full for all time in quiet order, for the remedy of our soul and of our kinsmen, as is contained in the precept of our most pious predecessors, and faithfully to obey our command and that of lord Arnulf. But so that this precept of our authority may obtain fuller force in the name of God, and may be more truly believed by the faithful of God's holy Church, namely in our present and future times, and be more diligently observed by our successors, we have confirmed it below with our own hand, with our princes, and have ordered it to be sealed with the impressions of our rings. Given on the third day before the Ides of November, in the year from the Lord's incarnation 623.
Dagobert, king of the Franks. Cunibert, archbishop of Cologne. Atto, bishop of Metz. Pippin, bishop of Speyer. Arnulf, duke of Mosellan Austrasia. Pippin, duke of Hesbaye, mayor of the palace.
IV.

Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he hands over to the basilica of Worms the property of his right in the district of Ladenburg, and confirms its possessions, with immunities (year 627).

Dagobert (Dagebert), king of the Franks. We wish all to know how we, thinking of the remedy of our soul and of future reward, have wholly resolved in our mind (sign) to make the churches of God co-heirs of our allodial lands, and to enlarge the places of the saints. On this we took the good counsel of our nobles: Pippin, who is mayor of the palace, Arnulf, bishop of Metz, Hunibert, archbishop (bishop) of Cologne; and we trust thereby to obtain the mercy of the Lord and to merit the intercession of his saints. Therefore, all you faithful of God and ours, present and future, recognise (know) how all (every) property of our right in the district of Ladenburg (Lobdengau), and whatever was seen to belong to our city, and everything that has hitherto pertained to our fisc, except the levy and the county, holding back nothing of it (nothing of it), we hand over entire and in full, great and small, to the basilica of St Peter (add.: and Paul) the apostle (add.: or of the other lords), which is built in the city of Worms, over which presides the lord (dom) apostolic man Amandus. This is what we hand over: our city of Ladenburg (Lobdenburg), our palace (omit 'our'), buildings, slaves, vineyards, lands cultivated and uncultivated, fields, meadows, plains, all (every) woodland right in the forests of the Odenwald, with every use throughout the district of Ladenburg (Lobdengau), and on all sides within (Jutraha), in pastures, timber, waters and watercourses, fisheries acquired and to be acquired, every toll, market, and whatever can be said or named; as it was formerly seen to belong to our use, so henceforth we have given it to the aforesaid basilica to possess, for the increase of eternal reward; and by our precept we confirm anew, under full community (immunity), all things pertaining to the same basilica, just as (as) in the previous year we gave protection of community (immunity) to all (and all) the estates, resources or abbeys, and whatever is seen to belong to the city of Worms itself: that no public judge, neither (nor to) for hearing cases, nor for exacting fines, nor for constraining the men of that church, free as well as servile, should dare (they should dare) to cause any obstruction; but that for the part (to the part) of that church, the bishop Amandus himself or his successors have (are held to have) it granted and allowed to possess and hold lordship (to lord it) in quiet order over what it was the custom to render to the parts of our fisc. And so that this authority may be firmer, we have decreed to strengthen it with our hand by the subscriptions set below. Dagobert (Dagebert), king of the Franks. Godefrid (Odefrid) recognised [it]. Given (omit 'Given') on the 2nd (11th) day before the Kalends of October, in the 6th year of our reign. Done at Mainz in our palace, most happily.
V.
Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he confirms the division of goods between Ursinus and his brother Beppolen (year 628).
Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man.

Whenever the petitions of faithful persons, in what they have laid open to our [ears], we are willing to hear them gladly one by one, and to bring them to effect in the name of God. And therefore our illustrious and faithful man, by God's favour, Ursinus has petitioned the clemency of our reign that, concerning what, together with his brother Beppolen, in the document of division, both from the inheritance of his father Chrodolen and of his brother Chaimedes, now deceased, the places whose names are Ferrarias, the hamlet Leubaredo and Eudoncovilla, or the remaining property, or those estates in Roteneco which are known to have come to them from the maternal allod by title of agreement: that is, with lands, buildings, slaves, vineyards, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movables and immovables, or other things or appurtenances pertaining to... [space of three or four letters], as has been said, had come to his share, and these at present were held in right order. Whence he affirms that he has in hand the fuller agreement concerning those places and the remaining things, subscribed by the hand of his aforesaid brother Beppolen, and the confirmation of good men.... [about four syllables missing], and likewise he affirms that he has in hand the sales by which he is seen to have [pur]chased certain portions in the aforesaid places from certain men [so on the bronze tablet; Mabillon reads 'purchased']: the aforesaid man petitioned that our precept should be confirmed more fully concerning him in this matter. His request, for the clearer firmness of the matter, we have not wished to refuse; for we order that whatever is established that he justly received in right order... [space of one letter] in the said places or other things to his share by the examined agreement, as against his aforesaid brother, in the division, and what he is known to possess through those sales in the aforesaid places, as he is seen at present to possess by right course, our authority in the name of God confirms in general, and he is to hold it [space of four syllables]... and leave it to his descendants to possess in perpetuity. And so that this authority may endure with firm stability for all time, we have decreed to strengthen it below with the subscriptions of our hand. Burgundofaro presented [it]. King Dagobert subscribed.
VI.
Precept of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he orders that Desiderius should take up the bishopric of Cahors (year 629).

Dagobert, king of the Franks, to the bishops and dukes and all the people established within the borders of the Gauls. It befits the clemency of our rule [the word 'our' is missing in Labbe] to pursue with shrewd inquiry and to handle with watchful care that our choice and disposition should accord in all things with the will of God; and since regions and kingdoms are known to have been joined to our power for ruling, by the Lord's bounty, the privileges of dignities should be entrusted to those whom a praiseworthy life and uprightness of character or nobility of birth raise up. And since we have come to know that the illustrious man Desiderius, our treasurer, has kept the observance of religion in all things from the very time of his boyhood, and under secular dress has borne himself as a soldier of Christ, and has angelic manners and a priestly way of life, so that the fame of his goodness, spread abroad, grows not only in neighbouring but also in distant regions, therefore we believe it right to advance him to the priesthood, whom, as we have said, adorned with good character, we see continually longing for the heavenly homeland; and since the consent of the citizens and abbots of Cahors demands in every way that they should have him as bishop, and our devotion likewise consents, we believe without doubt that this happens by God's will, so that, though he is very necessary to us in our palace, we do ourselves a kind of violence and procure him from our own household for the public benefit [Labbe: that we [procure] him from our household for your benefit]. But while, as we have said, we take him away from our household, we to whom regions and kingdoms have been entrusted by God, though we inflict loss on ourselves, we must procure such pastors as should rule the peoples entrusted to themselves and to us [better in Labbe: by us] according to God and the sayings of the apostles, whence a fuller reward may accrue to us. Wherefore, in accordance with the petition of the citizens and our will agreeing in all things, we decree and order that, with the Lord's help, with clergy and people acclaiming his praise, the illustrious man and true worshipper of God Desiderius be consecrated bishop in the city of Cahors, and that the will of ourselves and the citizens, what it has decreed, be accomplished in all things in the name of God and be exalted with the pontifical blessing; provided that, with Christ's favour, we profess with true religion that his life and conduct are held worthy and approved by all, to the extent that he should pray for us and for all the orders of the Church, and strive to offer acceptable sacrifices to God; for we believe that by this, the Lord granting it, our life is to be prolonged to a longer age, if he is chosen and exalted in the priesthood who may offer prayers securely before the tribunal of Christ for us and for you and those entrusted to him, and may stand by at the future judgement as an intercessor [Labbe: of sinners] to excuse faults. Wherefore by the present authority we decree that the often-mentioned Desiderius take up the bishopric in the city of Cahors forthwith, and, with Christ's favour, hold it in his time. And so that this deliberation of our will may be held firmer, we have decreed to strengthen it below with the subscription of our hand. Chrodobert presented [it]. King Dagobert subscribed. Given on the 6th day before the Ides of April [Labbe: on the day of the Ides of April], in the eighth year of King Dagobert.
VII.
Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he sanctions and establishes the Market of Saint Dionysius (year 629).

Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man, to the counts Leutho, Vulfio and Rauco, and to all our agents, vicars, *centenarii* [hundred-men] and the other ministers of our state. Let your solicitude and prudence know how we have willed and established, in honour of our lord and glorious patron Dionysius, the setting up of a market at his feast, which falls on the seventh day before the Ides of October, once a year, for all merchants residing in our kingdom or coming from beyond the sea, on the road that goes to the city of Paris, at the place called Pasellus of Saint Martin. And let our *missi* [envoys] know of this market, and all the cities in our kingdom, above all at the port of Rouen and the port of Wic, those who come from beyond the sea to buy wine and honey or madder; and for this year and the next, or before, the toll itself is to be remitted until the third year. And from then on, for each cartload of honey they are to pay two solidi for the bread of Saint Dionysius; and for each cartload of madder likewise two solidi; and the Saxons and the men of Wic and the men of Rouen, and the other country people from other cities, are to pay for their ship-dues twelve denarii for each cartload, and the *vultatici* and *passionatici* [dues], through all their successions and generations, according to ancient custom. We also order that this market be extended over four weeks, so that the merchants from Lombardy or Spain, and from Provence and from other regions, may be able to come there. And we will and expressly command that no merchant in the Paris district dare to trade except in the market which we establish or ordain in honour of Saint Dionysius; and if anyone does this, let him pay our ban for it to the share of Saint Dionysius. Finally we command, and expressly enjoin on you and on all agents, or your juniors or successors, present and to come, that the share of Saint Dionysius should never have any hindrance from that market on our part or yours, either within the city of Paris itself or outside in that district, concerning the tolls, or ship-dues, port-dues, bridge-dues, bank-dues, wheel-dues, *vultatici*, *themonatici*, *chespetatici*, dust-dues, market-dues, *mestatici*, *laudatici*, pack-load dues, *salutatici*: all things and from all things, whatever could be exacted for our share or the public fisc from that market out of its merchandise, let the share of Saint Dionysius or its agents have in perpetuity, by this our indulgence and authority. And so that this our precept may be held firmer for that holy place in our times and times to come, we have decreed to strengthen it below with the subscriptions of our hand, and have ordered it sealed with our ring. I, King Dagobert, have subscribed. Dado presented [it]. Given on the 3rd day before the Kalends of August, in the second year of the reign of Dagobert, at Compiègne, happily, in the name of God. Amen.
VIII.
Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he orders Sigibert, his cousin, to restore to Otho a castle situated in the Alps (year 630).

In the year of salvation six hundred and thirty, in the [reign of] Lothar II, eighth king of the Gauls, our father; the hundred and fifty-ninth [year] since the fall of the western empire; Heraclius the nineteenth emperor of the East; and Honorius the sixty-ninth Roman pontiff; on the fourth day of the month of May. We, Dagobert the Great, king of Austrasia and of the Burgundians, at the prayers of our mother Berentrude, queen of the Franks, having however first seen the most ancient tablets drawn up by the Roman emperors, [his] loyalty having always been preserved, and having also considered his origin, sprung from the Fabian family of most noble patrician blood, restore, give and confirm the castle situated in the Raetian Alps of Chur in Praevalia, which is called Castrum-Altum of the village of Pravanum, with all the rents and rights belonging to it, and also with the tithes from Mount Julius as far as the town of Oscela on the lake of Larius of the said Praevalia, to Otho, a vigorous man of the equestrian order, our officer, leader of soldiers against Ariovald, sixteenth king of the Lombards. Thus to you, Sigibert, our beloved cousin, first duke of Alemannia, we order, command and so will that you restore the above-mentioned castle to the above-named Otho, our officer, with all the things that belonged to it when it was seized from him, and that you establish him as vassal of all the things formerly held by his ancestors. In witness whereof, etc. Given in our castle of Isenburg.
IX. Letter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, that the consecration of Desiderius as bishop of Cahors should take place at the solemnity of Easter (year 630).

To the holy lord and apostolic lord, my father Pope Sulpicius, King Dagobert. As we well believe it is known to your holiness how our faithful man, the illustrious (Labbe: truly illustrious) Desiderius, our treasurer (Labbe: 'our' is lacking), has served us faithfully from the time of his youth, and we know well his most devout and monastic way of life; therefore know that we have decreed that in the city of Cahors, where his brother, the lord Rusticus, presided as bishop, he should receive in his place the honour of the episcopate in the name of God; for, by the inspiration of divine power, our devotion remains such that those whom we see adorned with good character and devoted to holy works, as is this Desiderius, most faithful to God and to us, these we ought to advance to the episcopal summit; for it so befits royal highness that those whom it knows to live in the fear of God, to keep the catholic faith intact, and to observe the precepts of the Gospel in every way, it should strive to promote to such an office. Accordingly, since we know that you hold the summit of metropolitan (Labbe: we know that you hold the place of archmetropolitan), we have taken care to send the present letter, with the due courtesy of greeting, to your kindness, asking that you hasten to bless him, and that you send letters to your fellow brethren of the province, so that they too may be present, in order that canonically and according to apostolic institution, in our presence, at the holy Easter solemnity, he may be confirmed with the pontifical blessing (Labbe: may be consecrated). This also we beseech above all, that you commend us to the Lord in your holy prayers pleasing to God, and make no delay in fulfilling the business we enjoin on you. This letter we have decreed to strengthen, as is the custom, with the subscription of our hand. King Dagobert subscribed.
X.
Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, concerning many churches built by him in honour of Saint Dionysius and made subject to the principal church of Dionysius (year 631).

Dagobert, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man, to archbishops, bishops and *actuarii* [officials]. Not unmindful of the benefits which the bounty of the supreme King has conferred through the merits of most blessed Dionysius, our special patron and protector, and also keeping before our eyes the condition of human frailty, indeed bearing in heart and mind a heartfelt love towards the same blessed Dionysius, and as the due fulfilment of that love, among the very many things we have conferred on his church, in which we wish to be buried, we have built many churches in our kingdom, which, dedicated in his honour and name, we have caused to be made subject to his principal church. One of these we built at the castle of Doué, on the border of Poitou and in the diocese of Anjou, and, consecrated to the name of the same most blessed martyr, we made it subject to his aforesaid principal church, together with two other churches built within the same castle, one in honour of Saint John the Baptist, the other in veneration of blessed Leodegar; and also two estates situated in the same diocese of Anjou, namely Sisiacum and Albiniacum, with two churches built on those estates and dedicated in honour and memory of the aforesaid most excellent martyr. We have also granted to blessed Dionysius whatever belongs to these five churches, with the revenue of all things whatever; for which reason we have ordered this precept of our highness to be made and given to the aforesaid Saint Dionysius and to the brothers serving the Lord there, so that they may hold and possess the said churches perpetually without anyone's opposition. And so that all things may be preserved unchangeably through all times, we have confirmed this our present authority with our own hand and have ordered it marked with our ring. [Sign] of Dagobert, most glorious king; of Louis, son of Dagobert; of Arnulf, bishop of Metz; of the bishop of Noyon, the most skilful goldsmith. Given by the hand of Dado, chancellor of the royal dignity. Done at Paris, happily, in the name of God. Given on the 4th day before the Ides of April, in the 12th indiction, in the 4th year of the reign of King Dagobert.
XI.
Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he confers the right of asylum on the monastery of Saint-Denis (year 632).

Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man, to all bishops, abbots, counts, *centenarii*, vicars and our other agents. Whatever we ordain in the present for the benefit and honour of the holy Church of God, and bring to effect, this we trust to be most necessary for us against visible and invisible enemies. Therefore we, in the name of God, sitting in a general synod in our palace of Clichy, together with the venerable bishops, abbots, counts and our other faithful men, have deliberated how the honour and praise of the church of the blessed martyrs, namely of our special patron the lord Dionysius and of his companions Rusticus and Eleutherius, might be maintained and observed; that is, that any fugitive, for whatever crime, fleeing to the aforesaid basilica of the blessed martyrs, who has reached the Tricena bridge, or, coming from the direction of Paris, has passed Montmartre, or, going out from our palace, has crossed the public road that leads to Luvera: just as God delivered us through these holy martyrs from the hands of our enemies and from the fury of the lord our father, so all who have fled there shall be freed and kept safe. For if almighty God, through the intercession of these saints, manifestly freed a brute animal, namely a stag, there in that holy place, much more is it fitting that rational men, for whatever offence of misdeed, whether they have committed some crime against us or the succeeding kings of the Franks, or against any other faithful man of the holy Church of God, should be released and freed. For we call to witness and adjure all our successors, kings or princes, by the holy and undivided Trinity and by the coming of the just Judge, that the honour and reverence of the holy mother church, where our lord and most holy patron Dionysius rests, be preserved in all things, just as the church of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul at Rome is known to hold [it] by the privilege of the emperor Constantine. But if anyone does not observe these things, let him be anathema both here and in the future. And so that this our authority may obtain fuller and firmer force in the name of God, we and our holy synod have decreed to strengthen it below with our own hand. Landeric presented [it]. King Dagobert subscribed. Bishop Laudomer consented and subscribed. Bishop Chrodobert consented and subscribed. Acterius, a sinner bishop, subscribed. In the name of Christ, Bishop Eligius subscribed. Bishop Rannemund subscribed. In the name of Christ, Bishop Sylvinus subscribed. Dado, bishop of the church of Rouen, consented and subscribed. Bishop Lorado consented. Bishop Mauricius consented. Palladius, a sinner bishop, subscribed. AEgynayvus subscribed. Clarus, in the name of God, subscribed. Ermenric, illustrious man, subscribed. Hubert, consenting, subscribed. Dado, a sinner, consented. Given on the 7th day before the Kalends of June, in the fifth year of the reign, at Clichy, happily, in the name of God. Amen.
XII.
Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he declares and confirms all the property belonging to the church of Saint Peter at Trier (year 632).

Dagobert, king of the Franks, to the illustrious men, dukes, counts, domestici, and all agents both beyond and on this side of the Rhine, or beyond the Loire, absent as well as present. We believe without doubt, in the name of God, that this serves the increase and stability of our kingdom: if, assenting to the right petitions of priests or of the churches of God, we bring to effect what they have laid open to our ears. Therefore the apostolic man, our father, the lord Modoald, archbishop of the church of Trier, brought to us a precept strengthened by the precepts of earlier kings, our predecessors and kinsmen, Sigebert, Theudebert, Theuderic, and indeed by the hands of Chlothar of good memory, the glorious king, our father. In it was set down that not only our father himself, but also his aforesaid predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks, confirmed by the authority of their precepts all the property whatsoever that good and holy men, out of regard for divine contemplation, had made over to the share of Saint Peter, the church of Trier, so that their kingdom might be protected by heavenly aid, and afterwards they themselves might rejoice in the heavenly kingdom with Christ without end. And so, for the security of the matter, the same aforesaid prelate Modoald begged our highness that, following the custom of our father and predecessors, we should order a precept of our authority of this kind to be made concerning the same property, for the love of God and reverence for Saint Peter. We gladly gave assent to his petition, and decreed that this precept of our authority be made for that church, for love of divine worship and for the remedy of our soul. By it we command and order that all the property and resources belonging to the church of Saint Peter of the city of Trier, namely the cell of Saint Hilary, which is now called [the cell] of Saint Maximin, which is built on the estate of Saint Peter, and the cell of Saint Paulinus and of Saint Eucharius, and the monastery of Saint Mary, which the same aforesaid bishop Modoald recently built from the foundation in the territory of Saint Peter, and which is called Horrea, the basilica of Saint Martin situated in the district of Maiginensis, and the other basilicas, forts, villages, estates, vineyards, woods, men, or whatever, by the bounty of divine clemency, shall hereafter be given to increase the same church, about the Rhine and the river Loire, lying in our kingdom, shall all remain perpetually made over under the right and power of Saint Peter, the church of Trier, and of its bishop. Moreover, in like manner we also decree that none of the public judges, nor anyone with judicial power, shall dare, in our times or in future times, to enter the monasteries, churches, forts, villages or fields, places, or other possessions of the aforesaid church, both beyond and on this side of the Rhine or the river Loire, in the districts or territories within the power of our kingdom which the said church possesses, or which divine power shall hereafter wish to be added to the right of that holy place, to hear cases, or to exact fines or tributes or any levies, or to take lodgings or provisions, or to take sureties, or to constrain the men of that church, or to seek unjust exactions, or to exact toll; nor shall they presume to exact at all any of the things mentioned above. But let it be lawful for the said prelate and his successors to possess in quiet order all the aforesaid monasteries, estates, villages and forts, with their appurtenances, whole for all time, for the remedy of our soul and of our kinsmen, as is contained in the precept of our most pious father, and faithfully to obey our command. And so that this precept of our authority may obtain fuller force in the name of God, and be more truly believed by the faithful of the holy Church of God, in our present and future times, and be more diligently preserved by our successors, we have confirmed it below with our own hand together with our leudes, and have ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring. Dagobert, king of the Franks... Cunibert, by the grace of God, archbishop of Cologne. Abbo, bishop of Metz. Principius, bishop of Speyer. Pippin, mayor of the palace.
XIII.
Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he gives to Sigiran the place Longoretum for building a monastery, and Milepecum for building a basilica (year 632).

When the Christian faith [Samm., 'of the Christian'] religion, to be dispensed by the apostles, the sacred teachers, with wonders and signs of miracles going before [Samm., 'premitibus'], was spread through the whole world with the name of Christ set first, a countless multitude of people of every condition flocked to the sacrament of baptism, to purify the harm of the old guilt. Clovis, then, king of the Franks, through the preaching of Saint Remigius [Samm., 'of Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims, by divine breath inspired, from him, first of the kings of the Franks, of baptism'], received the bath of baptism, of sacred purification. From him indeed I, Dagobert, son of King Chlothar, son of Chilperic, son of Chlothar, son of Childebert [Samm., 'son of King Chlothar, from the same Clovis'], from that same Clovis, the first of our line imbued with the faith of Christ, fifth, drawing my life's blood, a worshipper in my veins of the faith of Christ and of the undivided Trinity, at whose nod not even the stars resist, and whatever lies beneath heaven serves, holding dearer the cohabitation of the heavenly homeland, desire to increase with the property granted to me by God [Chop., 'by [his] nod'] the holy places endowed with relics of the saints and built by the holy imitators of the apostles, and also, in places where there was no memorial of Christ, to build foundations unwearied [Chop., 'there was no memorial of Christ in the places, unwearied']. For there is a place not far from the borders of the district of Poitiers or of Tours, very rich in pastures for herds and beasts of burden [Chop. adds 'countless'], watered by streams of water, and pleasant for hunting wild beasts, where I often had a mind to stay, which [Chop., 'indeed'] also, because of the frequent visits of kings for the sake of pleasure, is called Longoretum by those living there. It pleases me to give it to Sigiran, a kinsman of mine by birth, who, desiring to enjoy a happier life, removing himself from the archdeaconate of Tours, professes to me that he is passing the life he now lives under the monastic rule with brothers already joined to him. Therefore I, Dagobert, king of the Franks, at rest in tranquil peace by the foreordaining of divine clemency, with Clovis my son, with very many of my magnates present, give and grant, and confirm to be held in perpetual tenure, with royal power and dignity, this above-said place, set on the course of the Claise [Chop., 'Clasis'], and marked out in honour of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary [Chop., 'praenotato'], with the whole manor and the rights belonging to that manor, the churches, namely, with tithes and their dues, and all ecclesiastical revenue [Chop., 'jurisdiction'], and also whatever land, uncultivated or cultivated, or [revenue] from tolls on the public roads and pasture-dues of the woods, and also the head-tax from all [Chop., 'censis et omnibus'; Samm., 'and the tax from all'] the men belonging to that manor, indeed everything that appears to lie (from the course of the Indre to the crossing of the Creuse, around the borders of the territory of Bourges and of Poitiers, all of which lie in my lordship and own demesne [Chop. and Samm., 'dominico'] power, to Sigiran, son of Sigelaicus, count and bishop of Tours, so that he, son of the count of Bourges, renouncing worldly pomps, eager to please God by chastity, the guardian of virtues, may be allowed to build there from my own property and resources a cenobitic monastery, as he conceives in his mind), and that he may be pleased, with a fellowship of brothers devoting themselves to live for God under the regular order of monks [Chop., 'to vow themselves to God, protection'; Samm., 'devoting themselves to live there'], under the protection of the Mother of God, which is mightier than ours, to keep vigil in devoted [Chop., 'devotion'] service of the mysteries of God for his own salvation and that of our people. This place, then, foremost for me from the beginning of its construction [Samm., 'constructing'], we adorn with sacred protection [Samm. lacks 'sacred'] with part of the saving wood on which Christ suffered, and part of the garment of the Mother of God enclosed in gold, and part of the chin of John the Baptist, and with relics of other saints which we have from religious men, together with the entreating service of most honourable men, namely clerics and monks singing praises to God, so that the faithful people, coming here devoutly to pray, may know whose intercessions they ought to implore, God being gracious. (For to Clovis my son, whom I appoint to survive me in the kingdom of all Francia in tranquillity of peace and quiet, I commend, warn and command that if, as the number of monks living in this place grows, there should be need to add anything from our property or resources beyond what we give, he should not refuse to bestow it out of fatherly love [Chop. and Samm., 'love of me'], God rewarding him. And if anyone of our heirs or collateral kin, of relatives or of strangers, unable to restrain his envious fury, should presume to disturb or take away any of this, in the greatest or the least matter), he shall perish with the devil in the fire of Gehenna; or if he stands against Sigiran or the monks following him serving God and his holy mother Mary forever [Samm., 'him'], let royal vengeance await him, and moreover, worthy of the wrath of God, with those to whom he will say on the day of judgement, 'Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his ministers', let him be swallowed alive by the gaping of the earth with the two sons of Korah, namely Dathan and Abiram; or, hated by heaven and earth with Judas the traitor, reduced to dust, exposed to the whirlwinds, let him perish. For the security, then, of the perpetual tenure of this our gift, we command to be marked out the place which Sigiran says he has already foreseen [Chop., 'provided'] would be fit for building a basilica in honour of Saint Peter, which he also calls Millepecum [Chop., 'Mollepecum'], with all churches already built or to be built, and with all tithes as well as tolls and pasture-dues and levies, and all the issues of lands and woods, namely whatever there appears to be under cultivation or uncultivated, as has been said, within the bounds of the above-said border, so that kings coming after may recognise that they ought to be defenders and patrons of this royal monastery against every attack of persecutors, if anyone should presume to seize anything, as if by our gift or trust [Chop., 'fredo'; Samm., 'fief'] or by any fraudulent device. Indeed I, Dagobert, and Clovis my son, with royal power and dignity, with our own hands strengthen, authorise and confirm this gift to the holy [Samm., 'gift with devotion to the holy'] Mother of God and perpetual virgin Mary, in whose honour I command an altar to be made in my royal house, for celebrating the solemn sacrifice, until a more ample building is constructed. In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord six hundred and thirty-two, Vusseodus [Sammarth., 'Vulfoldus'] residing in the episcopal see of the city of Bourges; indiction 6, epact 11, moon 7. Sign of the lord Dagobert. Sign of Pippin, duke of the royal house. Sign of Ebroin. Sign of Clovis. Sign of Count Odo [Sammarth., 'Sign of Ebroin, Sign of Count Dodo'; so also Labbe]. Sign of Boso, chief keeper of the keys. Sign of Theuderic, precentor. Confirmed at Sigiran's dictation.
XIV.

Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which, after an inquiry has been made into the origins of the monastery of St Maximin (of Trier), he confirms the gifts and privileges granted to it, and himself confers new gifts (year 633).

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Let the diligence of all Christians know how I, Dagobert, most powerful king, by the agreed counsel of my bishops and counts, sent envoys on my behalf to Abbot Memilianus, commanding him to inquire diligently, and to inform me in person, by whose founding that monastery of St Maximin was built, or to whose authority it had been subject from former times. The abbot with the brethren received this embassy attentively, and when certain very ancient charters had been read through in that same place, it was found that the monastery itself had been a royal temple of the emperor Constantine, and that by his command it had been dedicated in honour of St John the Evangelist by St Agritius, the venerable bishop. In this temple, as the same father of the monastery disclosed to our royalty by a reliable report, at the request and with the support of Helena, the holy handmaid [of God], the above-said emperor gathered the poor of Christ, and set over them John, a man of God, so that they might always be free for the service of God and persevere in prayers for him; and moreover he would not subject the dwelling of that place to any other person, except to his own power and that of the emperors his successors. These things being firmly understood to be so, in royal manner I establish and by most firm command order that no one shall ever dare insolently to enter that monastery, over which the above-said abbot is seen to preside, or violently to inflict any inhumanity on it. Therefore, so that the remembrance of me and my forebears might remain continually in the aforesaid monastery, I have taken care to increase the provisions of those prebendaries of St Maximin, established under the aforementioned emperor, by adding estates on my part, whose names are these: Kannis, Cressiacum, Lunewich, Regiodola, Vallis Poliche, Baudeliacum, Talevant, Loavia. These places belong to the royal estate which is called Decima; this estate, with all things belonging to it, that is, whatever property I am seen to have from the river which is called Rubera as far as the forest which is called Leder, I have handed over to the holy bishop Maximin as a perpetual inheritance. Moreover, with the counsel and at the request of my princes, I have decreed for the companies serving God there this law, to be held firmly and perpetually hereafter: that the total of one hundred monks there shall always remain complete and unshaken; unless it be increased in estates or treasures by the benevolence of emperors or princes succeeding through the ages. And if, because of devastation by pagans or infidels or Christians, want beyond measure should fall upon these servants of Christ, and it cannot be driven off by spending treasure, let them have leave from God almighty and from me and my successors to give and to sell allodial land with its household, handed over by those faithful people, before the services of God are destroyed. And so that the confirmation of this charter may remain firm for ever, I have ordered it to be written out, and have confirmed it with our seal. Given on the day before the Nones of April, in the twelfth year of our reign, at Mainz, happily. Amen.
Sign of King Dagobert. I, Henry the chancellor, in place of Ricolf the arch-chaplain, have verified [this].
XV.
Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, for the foundation of the monastery of Haslach (year 633).

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen. Dagobert, by the favour of divine clemency, king of the Franks. To all the chief men of his kingdom, indeed to all who profess the Christian faith, future as well as present: grace to you, and peace from him who is, who was, and who is to come, the Almighty. The vow by which anyone has bound himself to God and the saints cannot be made void without the stain of guilt; and the greater and worthier he is to whom the vow is made, the heavier the judgement with which the presumption of one who vows and does not pay will be struck. We therefore ought and wish also to pay what we have vowed to the Lord God, the terrible, and to him who takes away the spirit of princes, terrible among all the kings of the earth (how he terrified us with the arm of his strength, and how, striking and healing, he visited us again, we have thought it fitting to make known to all as an example of correction, especially so that every faithful person, having heard of our peril, may refrain from laying waste the churches of God, and may show fitting honour to things dedicated to God. First, then, we shall set out briefly the divine examination held terribly upon us, and afterwards the vow and the paying of our vow. When my father Chlothar, of happy memory, died, I took up the care of my father's kingdom. But led by youthful levity, and distracted by desire for dominion, I neglected the duty of the royal office, showing nothing of the solicitude or diligence entrusted [to me], doing or judging nothing with gentleness or zeal for justice. Among my other excesses I had begun to be a destroyer and squanderer of churches, of which I ought to have been the defender and exalter, fearing neither the eyes of the divine majesty nor the outcry of men. At length the kindness of God, crushing the pride of my obstinate mind, visited my iniquities with the rod of correction, and did not deny me pardon once chastised. For, caught up on high and presented to the divine majesty seated in the guise of a judge among the choirs of the saints, I was gravely and persistently accused by the most holy patrons of the churches for ecclesiastical property carried off by plunder and consumed by me, above all by the most holy Mother of God, Mary, and by the receiver of souls, St Michael the archangel, and by the most blessed Peter and Paul, the chiefs of the apostles. And when, weighed down by conscience, I did not dare to defend my offences, by the decision of the one presiding I was condemned to punishments; and when I had long been beaten and worn out with atrocious punishments, the aforesaid archangel came, with a flaming sword stretched over me, wishing to exact vengeance on me for the goods usurped from himself and from the saints whom he had named, and because of the outcry of the needy and the poor, to whom I was hostile with the material sword, not judging right judgements. At length my special patron, the martyr Denis, came to my aid, making satisfaction for me to St Michael the archangel; by his prayers he obtained for me both a relaxation of the pressing punishment and time for penance. He himself, as if setting the measure of penance, placed for me the hope of full pardon in this: if, to the honour of God and of the aforesaid saints whom I had chiefly offended, I would build a house fit for divine services. Gladdened by this promise, I vowed willingly, and, released by those on high, I returned.) Therefore, in sure hope of pardon and remission of our sins, paying with eager zeal the vow that we made, I have built a monastery in honour of the holy Trinity and of St Mary, perpetual virgin, in the place called Hasela, situated in my kingdom and in the diocese of Strasbourg; and since the honourable Florentius, friend of God, then dwelling there in solitude, by the prompting of the divine Spirit requested it of us, we have decided to exalt the said monastery and enrich it with royal munificence. We therefore give to the aforesaid monastery, and wish it to be given in perpetuity, of the property of our fisc lying nearby, whatever pertains to us, in estates as well as slaves, woods, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses; and all these we bring by free donation to the use of the aforesaid monastery and of the brethren serving or ministering to God there, living however under the canonical rule. We also hand over to the venerable worshipper of God Florentius, and to his church, the place and valley within the bounds of the Vosges, which he faithfully chose for himself and his followers as a solitude or hermitage, and also for rest and for awaiting the general resurrection. But so that the servants of divine worship there, that is, in the aforesaid place and church, should not suffer any want or any lack of substance, we have handed over to them our well-ordered and well-managed royal residence of Kirckhaim with the outlying [lands of] Marley, the valley of Corona Virdenheim, the estate of Vege, the castle situated on the hill beside the Saverne road, as far as the stream Mosellus, with all adjoining hides, woods, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses. The place itself, which we embrace with singular love, we wish now and henceforth to be free from every oppression of servitude, under royal protection, in such a way that no public judge, no one of judicial power, shall presume to exercise any power or business in them, nor dare to constrain the men of the aforesaid places, either to hear cases or to pay fines or tributes, nor finally to exact anything at all from them. And so that this our handing over, and the institution of right and of the dignity granted, may remain continually stable and unshaken, we have arranged for this charter to be written about it, and have signed it, strengthened by the addition and hanging of our seal. (The gift we made, together with our sons, namely Clovis and Sigibert, in the said monastery of Haslach, the brethren there devoutly persevering in divine service. Present at this handing over were Nanthild, queen of the Franks, our lawful [wife], with our daughter Rathild. There were present also archbishops, bishops, abbots, provosts, dukes, margraves, palatines, counts, and very many princes of our kingdom. This was done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord six hundred and thirteen, in the month of April, on the sixteenth day, in the place often named.)
XVI.
Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he confers gifts and grants privileges on the church founded by him at Wissembourg (year 633).

Dagobert, by the favour of divine clemency king of the Franks, to all the chief men of his kingdom, indeed to all who profess the Christian faith, both future and present. A vow by which anyone has bound himself to God or to his saints cannot be made void without the stain of guilt; and the greater and worthier he is to whom the vow is made, the heavier the judgement with which the presumption of one who vows and does not pay will be struck. We therefore ought, and wish, also to pay what we vowed to the Lord God, the terrible one, and to him who takes away the spirit of princes, terrible among all the kings of the earth; and how he both terrified us with the arm of his power, and how, striking and healing, he visited us again, we have thought [it worthy] to make known to all, as an example of correction [M. B., exemplem], especially so that every faithful man, having heard of our peril, may restrain himself from laying waste the churches of God, and may show fitting honour to things dedicated to God. First, then, we shall briefly set out the divine examination terribly held over us, and afterwards [M. B., besides] the vow and the paying of our vow. When my father Lothar [M. B., Chlothar] of happy memory had died, I took up the care of my father's kingdom, but, led by levity of living and distracted by desire for domination, I neglected what was owed to the royal office, showing nothing of solicitude or diligence to those entrusted to me, doing or judging nothing with gentleness or with zeal for justice. Among my other excesses I had begun to be a destroyer and squanderer of the churches of God, of which I ought to have been the defender and exalter, fearing neither the eyes of the divine majesty nor the outcry of men. At length the kindness of God, crushing the pride of an obstinate mind, visited my iniquities with the rod of correction, and did not deny pardon to me once chastised. For, caught up on high and presented to the divine majesty, seated in the guise of a judge among the choirs of the saints, I was gravely and persistently accused by the most holy patrons of the churches for the church property scattered by plunder and consumed by me, above all by the most holy Mary, mother of God, and by the most blessed Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles. And since, burdened by conscience, I did not dare to defend my offences, I was by the decision of the one presiding sentenced to punishment; and when I had long been beaten and worn out by atrocious punishments, there came at last to meet me [M. B., came to my aid] my special patron, the martyr Denis, who by his prayers obtained for me a postponement of the impending punishment and a time for penance. He himself, as if setting the measure of penance, placed in this my hope of full indulgence: that I should build, to the honour of God and of the aforesaid saints whom I had most offended, a house fit for divine services. At this promise I gladly [M. B. adds: rejoicing] made the vow, and, dismissed by those above, I returned. Therefore, in sure hope of remission and indulgence of our sins, paying with eager zeal the vow we made, we have built a church in honour of the holy Trinity and of holy Mary ever virgin, and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, in the place called Wissembourg, which we have decided to exalt and enrich with royal munificence. We therefore give to it, and wish to be given in perpetuity, from the property of our fisc lying near there, whatever pertains to us, in estates as well as in slaves, woods, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses; and all these we bring by free handing-over into the use of the brethren serving God there under monastic profession. And so that the authority of this our donation may continue stable and firm for all time, we have taken care to note below the boundaries and the names of the surrounding places. Towards the eastern side the march which we have handed over extends as far as Marchenhofen [M. B., Morchenhevenum] and to Aldenherden, and thence to Geboldeswege, and thence below the ford [M. B., vatum] of the Lauter [M. B., Lutere], and thence Buozdingeshorste [M. B., Buezdingershurst], and thence to the boundary which stands at the top of the valley Invenesdal [M. B., Invensdal], and thence it leads to the southern side above Warspach, and thence to Bodemlosestompha [M. B., Bodemelosemstamph], and thence to Sebach, and thence to Kirchdale [M. B., Kirchendale], and thence to Ingoldeshare [M. B., Ingeldeshoche], and thence to the wooded hills as far as Bedebur; but on the western side as far as Lautenbach [M. B., Lutenbach] and Bernbach [M. B., Berenbach], and thence to Belebach [M. B., Erlibach], and thence to Gruneburnen [M. B., Grünenbrunnen], and thence to Otterichescheyt [M. B., Otterichschritt]; on the northern side as far as Eichenberg [M. B., Eychenberc]. And the place itself, which we embrace with singular love, we wish now and henceforth to be free from every oppression of servitude, under royal protection, in such a way that [M. B., ut] no public judge, no one of judicial power, shall presume to exercise or hold any power or business in that march without the leave of the father of the monastery, nor dare to constrain the men of that place, either to hear cases or to pay fines or [M. B., vel] tributes, nor finally to exact anything at all from them.

(This too we have decreed with equal authority: that none of the bishops of the city of Speyer, or of the other bishops, shall have any power of ruling there or of conducting any cases whatever, but that the father of the monastery with his brethren shall possess [M. B., possideat] freely and quietly, under the defence of our immunity, everything pertaining there [M. B. lacks sub]. In addition we grant to the same place a coinage bearing images and letters, and the express likeness of the coinage of Speyer; and by an equal donation of our authority we wish it to be ratified and firm that the men of the same church may attend freely to their business throughout all the bounds of our kingdom, in such a way that they pay the due of toll to no one [M. B., nulli], and that no judge or any person of whatever order shall presume [M. B., praesumat] to inflict any violence on them in a matter of this kind. And to the brethren [M. B., aut] serving God there, so that they may keep the order of their sacred [M. B., holy] way of life the more devoutly and tranquilly, we give free power of electing an abbot for themselves from among themselves. To this abbot, and to all succeeding him [M. B., ei], we grant this special privilege of dignity: that he may promote into the order and right of the ministeriales anyone of the household whom he judges worthy of such honour. All the ministeriales of the same church shall also receive their benefice by gift of the abbot [M. B., by the word of the abbot], and serve the abbot alone, nor shall the advocate dare to exercise any power over them, unless perhaps, on account of some disobedience, the abbot invites the advocate to constrain those [M. B., illos] ministeriales as rebels [M. B. lacks ad]. But the rest of the household ought [M. B., debent] to assemble at the advocate's court, at the lawful place and time, three times a year for justice to be done, and for the advocate's service, if he is present, each pay one penny, except those who are in the immunity [M. B., immunitate]. But if the advocate is absent from [M. B., ex] these courts, nothing of these pennies is owed to him, unless he is proved to be in the service [M. B., servitiis] of the king.

And so that this our handing over, and the institution of right and of the dignity granted, may remain continually stable and unshaken, we have signed this written charter, strengthened by the addition of our seal. The gift we made, in the monastery itself, in the month of May, on the eleventh day, in the twenty-third year of our reign, happily in the name of Christ. Amen.)
XVII.
Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, on the foundation of the church of the Cross of Saint Ouen (year 633).

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Dagobert, son of Chlothar the younger, king of the Franks, when after the death of my father of most glorious and most excellent [memory, supplied], king of the Franks, I was flourishing in the kingdom, and all things round about, subjugated to our dominion, were quiet, on a certain day of the month of May, together with the nobles and the chief men of the palace, in the forest of Cuise, as was customary.... [So in the copy]. But while we were all with one mind eagerly intent on taking a wild beast, and each was running here and there through the shady glades in pursuit, suddenly the lord Ouen, our archchaplain, came upon a certain pleasant but narrow level space, in which he found in the snow the image of the Lord's cross, the ground unmarked; for both yesterday and the day before there had been great clearness of the sky, and the sun with unbridled chariots was sweeping over the lands with its bright light. He saw, he stood still, he froze, and, retracing his course, hastening all the way to us, he reported it. We hurried [there], as he had said. We too saw, we marvelled, we acknowledged that it was so great a portent. Therefore the same lord Ouen, being most prudent, knowing that the same place was visited and frequented by the Lord, throwing himself at our knees, asked that it be given to him for building a basilica; and he deserved to obtain it, from the river Oise opposite Gallis-Villa, with a great extent of woodland and lands lying round far and wide, as far as Bellumvillare, and as far as the bank of the same river, namely opposite Ripparii curtis; there he built a church in honour of the holy Cross, and also gathered a small village; and finally, with our leave and will, he gave it to Saint Medard, for love of the brethren with whom he had been brought up there from the very first elements of childhood and educated in liberal studies, not moderately but perfectly. At his own humble request we made it free from the lordship, advocacy, bans and customary dues of all. And so that it may remain firm, we ordered this letter to be made in testimony, and, in the presence of bishops, counts and palatines, marked with our name, we confirmed it with the impression of our ring. Sign of Dagobert, renowned king of the Franks. S[ign] of Flavius, archbishop of Reims. S. of Sulpicius, archbishop of Bourges. S. of Ambrose, bishop of the Gabali. S. of Faro, bishop of Meaux. S. of Amandus, bishop of Maastricht. S. of Eligius, bishop of Noyon. S. of Lebunius, bishop of Chartres. S. of Amalarius, bishop. S. of Maurinus, bishop. S. of Erchinoald, mayor of the palace. S. of Beroald, noble of the palace. S. of Aigulf, count. S. of Bertin, knight. S. of Werchemar, knight. S. of Authar, knight. S. of Rado, knight. I, Ouen, chancellor, wrote and subscribed.

XVIII. Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he gives the castle of Saint Denis to the monastery of Saint-Denis (year 633). Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man, to Mummolus the prefect, and to Gondoen, Werpen, Dructoald, Auclin, Charimund and Chariulf, counts, and to all agents, present and future. It is fitting for us to watch above all over those things which concern the glory of God and the honour of his Church, and to bring them to a good end, so that we may thereby deserve to obtain our salvation. Since, then, we have quite often had our residence in the castle of Saint Denis, and, staying there as if in our own palace, held our solemn court on feast days, and this was a hindrance to the brethren, the monks who serve God there, it has pleased our serenity, on the advice of our faithful men, to withdraw from that castle, and henceforth to transfer that court on those feasts elsewhere, though not far from that castle, namely to our palace of Clichy, so that, the church of our patron the great Denis remaining untroubled by all disturbance, no worldly noise may hinder the brethren from being able continually and more attentively to entreat the Lord's mercy for us. Using therefore sound counsel, with the consent of the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and the magnates and nobles of our kingdom, we have decreed and ordained, adjuring by the holy and undivided Trinity and by the coming of the just Judge, that from this day forward, for the honour of God and out of reverence for our glorious protector and patron the lord Denis, neither we nor our successors shall in any way make our residence any longer in the aforesaid castle and holy place, where, I say, the lord Denis himself rests in the body and where we wish to be buried, nor shall we celebrate or hold our solemn court there on the solemn days of Easter, Pentecost, Christmas and Epiphany; but just as Constantine the Great, emperor ever august and most secure defender of the holy catholic Church, under whom it flourished and grew in a wonderful way, offered to blessed Peter the citadel of the Roman empire in its entirety and conferred it on Saint Sylvester by his lawful documents, so we too, by our royal munificence, grant in perpetuity and give to God and to blessed Denis, our special protector, this castle with all its adjacent lands and appurtenances, without any counter-claim; and whatever our fisc could have expected from it we confirm by this decree to that holy place and to the brethren, the monks serving God there; and those who presume to attempt anything against this our authority and our decree are to be subjected to and struck with the bond of anathema by the archbishops and bishops.
